clue.text: Centralised arrangement for employment qualifications

indicators.note: an arrangement puts things into a new order, so the letters are laid out afresh

parts.note: taken as written, eleven letters of raw material

explanation.surface: A centralised system for handling the qualifications people need to get jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centralised arrangement' reads as a bureaucratic scheme, but the first word supplies every letter and the second rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: Credentials are the documents and certificates proving someone is suited to a job or position.

clue.text: I'm taken aback and largely ill on a French island

parts.note: 'Cor!' is a British exclamation of surprise, what you say when taken aback

indicators.note: largely means most of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: ill means sick

explanation.surface: Someone reels back, feeling rather unwell, on an island off France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cor!' is a British expression of surprise. SICK with 'largely' loses its last letter to give SIC; 'on' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Corsica is a Mediterranean island governed as a region of France.

clue.text: Needs hem altering, being tangled up

indicators.note: altering something changes its form, so the letters take a different order

parts.note: taken as written, eight letters

explanation.surface: A garment whose hem needs altering because the thread has got all tangled.
explanation.walkthrough: The sewing picture hides that 'Needs hem' supplies all eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To be enmeshed is to be caught as if in a net, entangled and unable to get free.

clue.text: Eagle — rather nautical eagle, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of each word counts

parts.note: the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A musing on whether a particular eagle might be the seafaring sort.
explanation.walkthrough: The first word is both the definition and part of the material; read whole, the clue describes the bird, a sea eagle, so it is a semi-&lit.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed sea eagle, a crossword favourite because of its handy letters.

clue.text: Tantalised by a little bird, I will have dined on starter of duck

parts.note: the tit is a small songbird
contracted to I'LL
dined means ate

indicators.note: a starter is what comes first in a meal, so just the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A diner tempted by small game birds, about to start on duck.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'on' places the duck's letter after the dining; the apostrophe of I'LL disappears, as punctuation always does in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Titillated and tantalised both mean excited or teased, often with a promise of pleasure.

clue.text: Rattle and bell, often

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to unsettle or frighten someone
second meaning: a warning device, frequently a ringing bell

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rattle and bell' look like two noisy objects, but the first is a verb meaning to unnerve.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for frightening someone and a noun for a warning signal that commonly rings.

clue.text: A little barista in Edinburgh is covered in blotches

indicators.note: a little of something is only a portion, so the letters are a run taken from within the words

parts.note: the run spans all three words

explanation.surface: A coffee-shop worker in Edinburgh is splattered with spills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A little barista' suggests a small person; it means a little piece of the following words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stained bears marks or discoloured patches, the sort left by coffee or ink.

clue.text: Unhealthy cornet cut out, assuming bachelor's wanting vegan fare

indicators.note: something unhealthy is in poor shape, so the letters are jumbled into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, twelve letters
B is the standard abbreviation for bachelor

explanation.surface: An unhealthy ice-cream cornet is cut from the diet of a bachelor who wants vegan food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assuming' means taking on, so the bachelor's letter joins the mix before the shuffle; 'cut out' is part of the material, not a deletion.
explanation.definitionFit: Coconut butter is a plant-based spread made from coconut flesh, suitable for people avoiding animal products.

clue.text: Regrettably, a tour fell flat making you nervous

indicators.note: regrettably signals something gone wrong, so the letters come out badly arranged

parts.note: taken as written, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: A tour that flopped leaves the performer anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of the four middle words is used once.
explanation.definitionFit: Being all of a flutter is an idiom for being agitated, excited or jittery.

clue.text: Ransome's written about a group in a boat

definitions.note: a singular collective defining a plural noun

indicators.note: something written about is moved around on the page, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the author's surname taken as written

explanation.surface: Arthur Ransome, author of Swallows and Amazons, wrote about children sailing in boats.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: Ransome's best-known books are about children in small boats on the Lakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Oarsmen are the rowers who crew a boat, collectively a group pulling oars together.

clue.text: Revolutionary painting? Very upset: it's hard work

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns round completely, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: a painting is a work of art
V is the abbreviation for very
to ail is to trouble or upset

explanation.surface: Someone distressed by a revolutionary painting complains that art is hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an anagram signal but supplies a word of its own, the verb ail.
explanation.definitionFit: Travail is an old-fashioned word for painful or laborious effort, toil.

clue.text: Leaves out some whom I.T. suggests

indicators.note: some means only part of the whole, so the letters lie within the following words

parts.note: the run spans the three words, ignoring the full stops

explanation.surface: The IT department suggests which staff get left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The full stops in I.T. are punctuation and vanish, leaving the letters to run on.
explanation.definitionFit: To omit is to leave something out, exclude or fail to include it.

clue.text: Blasted duck — or beautiful bird

parts.note: both are mild British curses, as in 'flaming nuisance'
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so the zero shape

explanation.surface: Someone cursing a wretched duck while admiring a lovelier bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' wants to be the bird; it is cricket's score of zero. 'Blasted' looks like an anagram signal but is simply the curse word.
explanation.definitionFit: Flamingos are tall pink wading birds, widely admired for their striking colour.

clue.text: Minister having disagreement about church to speak with delicacy

indicators.note: to be about something is to be around it, so one part goes round another

parts.note: a common abbreviation for minister
to have words is to argue
the Church of England

explanation.surface: A government minister quarrelling over church matters.
explanation.walkthrough: The church letters sit between the other two pieces, which wrap around them.
explanation.definitionFit: To mince words is to soften what you say, avoiding bluntness out of tact or caution.

clue.text: United appoint endlessly wealthy Australian dietician, ultimately opposed to apple pie?

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names
to name someone is to appoint them to a post

indicators.note: endlessly means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: wealthy means rich

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very last letter of the word dietician

parts.note: its final letter is N

explanation.surface: A sports team signs up a rich Australian nutritionist who frowns on pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As American as apple pie' is the idiom, so something opposed to apple pie is cheekily opposed to American values; the question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple pie symbolises the American way of life, so whatever rejects it is contrary to American values.

clue.text: Everyman finally did change a lightbulb — in a manner of speaking

definitions.text: a lightbulb — in a manner of speaking

parts.note: the setter speaking of themselves

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so the last letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the closing letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A lightbulb joke: how many setters does it take to change one? Everyman finally did.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's name stands for 'I', the setter; 'finally' applies to the words after it, not to the name.
explanation.definitionFit: In cartoons a sudden thought is drawn as a lightbulb over the head, so the bulb figuratively stands for inspiration.

clue.text: Protection from wind given to top pilot in film

parts.note: a scarf keeps a cold wind off the neck
an ace is an expert fighter pilot

explanation.surface: A star pilot is handed a scarf against the wind in some aviation movie.
explanation.walkthrough: Classic flying aces wore silk scarves, which makes the surface vivid.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarface is a gangster movie, made in 1932 and remade in 1983 with Al Pacino.

clue.text: Friends: they'll give you flowers

definitions.meaning: first meaning: pals, short for buddies
second meaning: the unopened shoots that later bloom

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests friends bringing a bouquet; the second half describes what plants produce before flowering.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is American slang for close pals and also names the swellings on a stem that open into blooms.

clue.text: Chump and onion that's hard to see?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, whimsically: an onion is a bulb, and a faint one is hard to make out

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the second reading is a stretch: a bulb can be a plant bulb like an onion, not just a lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupid person is informally called a lacklustre lamp, and an onion is botanically a bulb that could be faint.

clue.text: Mountain rock by cape; piercing yell — who's making it?

parts.note: scree is loose rock on a mountainside
C is the map abbreviation for cape
a howl is a long loud cry

explanation.surface: A shrill cry echoes off the rocks of a mountain headland, and someone asks who is making it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points back at the wordplay: the yell just described is the bird's call, a pleasing twist on whodunnit.
explanation.definitionFit: Screech owls are named for their shrill cries, so the bird is literally the one producing the piercing yell.

clue.text: Shore up revival for legendary musician

indicators.note: a revival is a new staging or form, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, seven letters

explanation.surface: An attempt to prop up a comeback for a famous old performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shore up' reads as a verb phrase, but it is only the raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Orpheus was the Greek mythical lyre player whose music charmed even the gods of the underworld.

clue.text: Male bird of prey one captured with weapon

indicators.note: captured means the male bird holds the letter for one inside it

parts.note: a tom is a male animal, especially a cat
a hawk is a bird of prey
A means one, as in 'a dozen'

explanation.surface: A cock raptor has seized something, along with a hatchet.
explanation.walkthrough: TOM and HAWK side by side hold A between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomahawk is a light axe used by Native North Americans as a tool and weapon.

clue.text: Doesn't show animals' skin

definitions.meaning: first meaning: conceals, keeps out of sight
second meaning: the pelts of beasts, as used for leather

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one statement about camouflage; it splits into a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for concealing something and a plural noun for animal pelts tanned into leather.

clue.text: Provide new container for flipping drunkard

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the word runs the other way

parts.note: a toper is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: Someone finds a fresh bottle for a bloody drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British curse on the drunkard; it is the turnaround signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To repot a plant is to move it into a new or larger pot as it grows.

clue.text: Superstar's out of work, we're told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: idle means not working

explanation.surface: Rumour has it a celebrity is now unemployed.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words sound alike in most accents.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is a hugely admired celebrity, someone fans worship like a god.

clue.text: Land in trouble tucking into dodgy cure

indicators.note: to tuck into is to go inside, so one piece is placed within another
something dodgy is unreliable or crooked, so the letters are not in their proper order

parts.note: taken as written
ado means fuss or bother

explanation.surface: Someone lands in trouble after trying a dubious remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Land in trouble' wants to be a phrase; 'Land' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecuador is a South American country, and land is a common crossword word for nation.

clue.text: No longer working, detective, unerring marksman

parts.note: a dead battery or machine no longer works
a private eye is a detective

explanation.surface: A retired detective who was a crack shot.
explanation.walkthrough: Detective often gives DI in crosswords, but here it is the eye of private eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadeye is a supremely accurate shot, someone who never misses a target.

clue.text: Blockbusting books from footballer and comedian

parts.note: George Best was a famous Manchester United and Northern Ireland footballer
Peter Sellers was a British comic actor, of Goon Show and Pink Panther fame

explanation.surface: A sports star and a comic both publishing hit memoirs.
explanation.walkthrough: Celebrity autobiographies are often blockbusters, so the picture holds together.
explanation.definitionFit: Bestsellers are titles that sell in huge numbers, the publishing equivalent of a blockbuster film.
